body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students understand that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for tens and ones (1.NBT.B.2).
- Students understand 10 as a bundle of ten ones, the numbers 11 to 19 as a ten and some ones (1.NBT.B.2b), and 10, 20, 30 ... 90 as some tens and 0 ones (1.NBT.B.2c).

MATERIALS
- Straws or craft sticks and rubber bands, for bundling tens
- The class counting collections (buttons, pasta, bottle caps) in bags of 20 to 60
- Base-ten rods and cubes, or connecting cubes snapped in trains of ten
- A tens and ones mat (two columns) for each student
- Tablets with the class activities open, for photos of work

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Bundles of Ten together. Each pair counts a counting collection by making groups of ten in cups. Record: how many tens? how many ones left? how many in all?
Day 2: Lesson activity: Sam's Straws. Read the story aloud, then rebuild it with real straws and rubber bands. Students answer, then tell a partner why counting by tens is faster.
Day 3: Tens and Ones. Students build each number on a tens and ones mat, then show their work. Spend time on 50 (5 tens and 0 ones) and the teen number 17.
Day 4: Draw It With Tens. Model quick drawings: a stick for each ten, a dot for each one. Students draw 26 and 41 and record themselves telling the tens and ones.
Day 5: Assessment: Tens and Ones Check. Read each problem aloud. Students may use cubes and their mats. Watch for students who reverse the digits (writing 74 for 7 ones and 4 tens).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: keep to numbers under 50 and always build with real objects before drawing. Use a mat with a picture of a ten-stick at the top of the tens column.
- Support: for teen numbers, start with a full ten frame plus some loose counters.
- Stretch: ask for a number shown two ways (34 is 3 tens and 4 ones, or 2 tens and 14 ones) and numbers to 120 (11 tens is 110).
- Multilingual learners: say "tens" and "ones" while touching the bundle and the single straw every time. Note that teen number names in English hide the ten (eleven, twelve) and say the ones first (fourteen); many languages say "ten-four". Invite students to count in their home language and compare.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are learning that big numbers are made of tens and ones: 34 is 3 tens and 4 ones. Please send in a small bag of buttons, pasta or bottle caps for our counting collections if you can. At home, count a pile of something together by making groups of ten. Ask your child: how many tens? How many left over? How many in all?
title: Teacher guide: Tens and Ones
